title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the median age across counties in Florida, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

   <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>

section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                     myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida    32.2    0.2  281751    NA
2 12003 Baker County, Florida      38.1    0.7   28186    NA
3 12005 Bay County, Florida        41.4    0.3  181368    NA
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida   40.5    1.2   27888    NA
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida    46.8    0.2  620533    NA
6 12011 Broward County, Florida    41.3    0.2 1946127    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         59        369666.
2 Low confidence           2          7842.
3 Moderate                 6         17153.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]
The average population of high-confidence counties is 337126 in 65 counties, while the average population of low-confidence is 7842 in 2 counties. It means that larger population sizes have higher data confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]

In Florida, the communities we know the least about are small, rural counties such as Lafayette County and Liberty County. In our analysis, Lafayette County had the highest relative margin of error at 6.22%, while Liberty County, Florida have the margin of error at 5.37%. This two counties also fell into the moderate confidence category, with an average population of just 7,842.
This uncertainty stems directly from how the American Community Survey (ACS) operates. Because the ACS collects data from a sample of households rather than conducting a full census count, smaller populations naturally yield smaller sample sizes. With fewer completed responses, individual sample variations will lead to higher random variations on a bigger impact, driving up the margin of error percentage relative to the estimate.
If a state agency allocated funding based on median ages, like distributing senior services grants. Treating every county’s estimate as equally certain means that the rural residents would suffer most. In small counties, less sample calculated median age. If Lafayette County’s median age were underestimated due to sampling error and there is more outliner, state algorithms might misclassify it as a younger community and withhold essential funding for senior centers, elder healthcare, and specialized transit. Meanwhile, large urban counties like Miami-Dade have massive sample sizes, negligible relative error, and stable funding streams. Relying uncritically on ACS estimates without accounting for margin of error disproportionately harms vulnerable, small-town communities by compounding statistical uncertainty with financial deprivation.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
I use B17001_002, the number of people whose income in the past 12 months was below the poverty level, divided by B17001_001, the population for whom poverty status is determined. The denominator is the population covered by this poverty table, rather than the entire population from a separate table. I use the same variables in both periods so that the rates measure the same thing. The Week 3 notes identify B17001_002 as a poverty count; I adapt the practice script’s moe_prop() calculation to this table. The E columns contain estimates and the M columns contain their margins of error.
I request survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 and year = 2017, which represent 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. text:
Part 2 — Test

Calculate rates and investigate missing values
I combine the two downloads with a period label, then apply the same calculation to every tract-period row. Multiplying both the proportion and its MOE by 100 expresses the rate as a percentage and the MOE in percentage points. I check the original counts before calculating rates: a zero denominator makes a rate undefined, rather than making it a zero-poverty tract. Missing or invalid inputs remain unavailable.


Show code
poverty_rates <- bind_rows(
  acs_2006_2010 %>% mutate(period = "2006-2010"),
  acs_2013_2017 %>% mutate(period = "2013-2017")
) %>%
  mutate(
    input_status = case_when(
      is.na(total_popE) | is.na(total_povertyE) |
        is.na(total_popM) | is.na(total_povertyM) ~ "Missing count or MOE",
      total_popE == 0 ~ "Zero poverty-universe population",
      total_popE < 0 | total_povertyE < 0 |
        total_povertyE > total_popE |
        total_popM < 0 | total_povertyM < 0 ~ "Invalid count or MOE",
      TRUE ~ "Usable"
    ),
    # NA prevents division by zero while preserving the original counts.
    denominator = if_else(input_status == "Usable", total_popE, NA_real_),
    pov_rate = 100 * total_povertyE / denominator,
    pov_rate_moe = 100 * moe_prop(
      total_povertyE, denominator, total_povertyM, total_popM
    ),
    # CV is undefined for a zero rate; its rate and MOE can still be used.
    cv = if_else(pov_rate > 0,
                 (pov_rate_moe / 1.645) / pov_rate * 100, NA_real_),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(pov_rate) | is.na(pov_rate_moe) ~ "Unavailable rate or MOE",
      pov_rate == 0 ~ "CV undefined: zero rate",
      cv < 12   ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40  ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE      ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

  filter(input_status != "Usable")

This explains their undefined rates; the counts alone do not identify their land use or prove that their total resident population is zero. I retain these rows in the audit and exclude a tract from the change test if either period lacks a usable rate or MOE.


Match tracts and test changes
I join by GEOID, following the Week 4 notes. A full join keeps unmatched identifiers visible. Change is the later rate minus the earlier rate, in percentage points. Following the practice script, I divide each MOE by 1.645 to get its standard error, combine the two standard errors, and multiply by 1.645 for the MOE of the change. A change is detectable at 90% confidence when abs(z) > 1.645, meaning its interval excludes zero. Reliability describes the precision of an individual rate; it is separate from this test of change.


Show code

  filter(period == "2006-2010") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2010 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2010 = pov_rate_moe)

  filter(period == "2013-2017") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2017 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2017 = pov_rate_moe)

unmatched_2017 <- anti_join(selected_2017, selected_2010, by = "GEOID")

  mutate(
    change = pov_rate_2017 - pov_rate_2010,
    se_1 = pov_moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2 = pov_moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = if_else(se_diff > 0, change / se_diff, NA_real_),
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      is.na(significant) ~ "Not testable",
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Detectable increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Detectable decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  )

    detected = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detected = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    excluded = sum(is.na(significant)),
    increases = sum(result == "Detectable increase"),
    decreases = sum(result == "Detectable decrease"),

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
Supported: the broader idea that poverty rates increased in some Philadelphia areas is consistent with the tract evidence: 36 tracts have detectable increases. Change is not uniform, however; 27 tracts have detectable decreases. Not supported: interpreting every positive estimate as established worsening would go beyond the evidence. Of 211 positive changes, only 36 pass the 90% test, and 313 testable tracts overall have intervals that include zero. This is a limit on what can be inferred from the estimates, not evidence that the article explicitly claimed every tract worsened or that every non-detectable change is actually zero.
Cannot be determined: the specific claim that Eastwick rose from 12% to 26%, and especially that its increase was the largest among neighborhoods, cannot be established or contradicted by these tract results. The assignment says the article’s neighborhood groupings are unavailable. A neighborhood rate would require the appropriate aggregated counts and their uncertainty, not an average of tract percentages. A tract with an increase above 14 percentage points would not disprove Eastwick’s neighborhood ranking because tracts and neighborhoods are different units. This report also makes no finding about the article title’s racial comparisons: the two variables used here describe poverty for the full poverty universe, without a race breakdown.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty changes were uneven between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Among 376 census tracts with usable estimates, 36 showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty rates and 27 showed a detectable decrease at 90% confidence. Changes in the other 313 tracts were too uncertain to distinguish from zero. Another 8 tracts could not be compared because their poverty rates were undefined in at least one period. These findings support increases in some parts of the city, but they do not establish Eastwick’s reported rise from 12% to 26% or its ranking among neighborhoods. Checking those claims requires the tract groupings used to define each neighborhood.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
A linear model draws straight lines through the features it receives. Feature engineering changes or adds predictors so that a linear model can represent skew, curves, group differences, and place-level variation.
The lecture evaluates changes by cross-validated RMSE, not by p-values. To compare models fairly, use the same observations and the same cross-validation folds throughout.








Feature change
What it can do for predictions
How to read coefficients




Log
Handle skew and nonlinear scaling
Often changes the unit to a percentage interpretation


Squared term
Let a relationship curve
The linear and squared terms must be interpreted together


Category
Represent groups or jumps
Each coefficient compares a group to a reference


Interaction
Let a slope vary by group
The effect depends on the group


Fixed effect
Account for unmeasured differences among places
Describes adjusted place differences; it does not explain their causes

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.1 Why log?
Income and rent can be right-skewed. A few very high values can pull a straight-line fit. A log compresses the upper tail and makes equal percentage changes comparable distances. For example, moving from $20,000 to $40,000 may matter more than moving from $180,000 to $200,000, even though both changes are $20,000.

3.1.1 Log a predictor
f_logx <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m_logx <- lm(f_logx, data = tracts)

b <- coef(m_logx)["log(income)"]
b / 100             # approximate rent change for a 1% income increase
b * log(1.10)       # exact model-implied change for a 10% increase
In a level–log model (y ~ log(x)), a 1% increase in x is associated with approximately β / 100 units of y, holding other variables constant.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.2 Zeros: log1p()
log(0) is negative infinity. This causes problems for variables that can be zero, such as counts of crimes, trees, or 311 calls. Use log1p(x), which calculates log(x + 1):
log1p(c(0, 1, 10, 100))
The percentage interpretation is approximate, especially for small values.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.3 Log the outcome
f_logy <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m_logy <- lm(f_logy, data = tracts)
In a log–level model (log(y) ~ x), a one-unit increase in x is associated with approximately 100 × β percent change in y. For a larger coefficient, calculate the exact percentage as (exp(β) - 1) × 100.
In a log–log model (log(y) ~ log(x)), β is an elasticity: a 1% increase in x is associated with approximately a β% change in y.







Model form
Approximate coefficient interpretation




Level–level: y ~ x
+1 unit of x → β units of y


Level–log: y ~ log(x)
+1% of x → β / 100 units of y


Log–level: log(y) ~ x
+1 unit of x → about 100 × β% change in y


Log–log: log(y) ~ log(x)
+1% of x → about β% change in y



RMSE trap: RMSE must be on the same outcome scale to compare models. A residual RMSE from a model of log(rent) is in log-dollars; it cannot be compared with the baseline RMSE in dollars. During cross-validation, exponentiate predictions before calculating RMSE. Directly exponentiating a predicted log often estimates closer to the median than the mean, so it can underpredict somewhat; the lecture treats this simple back-transformation as adequate for the assignment.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
7.1 Fixed effects and cross-validation
A fixed effect can only predict groups represented in the training data. If a district is absent from a training fold, its coefficient is unavailable and prediction can fail. Count group sizes before cross-validation. The lecture’s rule of thumb is around 10 or more observations per group for 10-fold CV, with more being safer.
Possible responses to very small groups:

Merge them with a geographically or substantively sensible neighbor (preferred when defensible).
Lump small groups into “Other” for a quick solution, while recognizing the group may combine unrelated places.
Use a coarser geography.

The example merges small districts with nearby districts for the CV predictor. It emphasizes that FE is a kind of place memorization and cannot generalize to a never-seen place.







Fixed effects
Spatial features




Capture unmeasured differences associated with a group
Represent measured conditions such as proximity to transit, parks, or crime


Cannot predict an unseen group
Can be computed wherever the feature is available


Group boundaries and scale are inherited
Feature scale can be chosen


Tell you where adjusted differences are
Help describe what may explain differences



They can complement each other: spatial features explain measured conditions, while FE can account for remaining place-level differences.

    renter_occ = "B25003_003",   # renter-occupied units
    edu_total  = "B15003_001",   # population 25+
    ba         = "B15003_022",
    ma         = "B15003_023",
    prof       = "B15003_024",
    phd        = "B15003_025"
  ),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)          # Pennsylvania South State Plane, feet

Now build the variables. A data frame goes in, a data frame comes out.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    pct_renter = renter_occE / occ_unitsE * 100,
    pct_ba     = (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / edu_totalE * 100,
    rent_se    = med_rentM / 1.645,
    rent_cv    = rent_se / renter_occE * 100

Bring back the stations and count how many sit within half a mile of each tract. This is Week 4 with one new function.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(philly_tracts))

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_is_within_distance(., stations, dist = 2640)))

Stop and look: st_is_within_distance() returns a list, one element per tract, holding the stations within range. What does lengths() do to that list?

Which tracts can we model?
A regression can’t use a row with a missing Y or X. R will quietly drop those rows, and later your residuals won’t line up with your tracts. So drop them yourself, on purpose, and count.

nrow(philly_tracts)

tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0,
         !is.na(med_rentE),
         !is.na(med_incE),
         !is.na(pct_ba),
         !is.na(pct_renter))

nrow(tracts)

Rule from Week 4, again: how many tracts did you lose? Which kind of tract has no median rent? (Hint: think about who lives there.)

WarningTwo different CVs

6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[___, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = ___)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $___ per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = ___)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

cv_m1$results
cv_m2$results

Setting the same seed before each train() gives both models the same folds, so the comparison is fair.

section: Part 7: Where is the model wrong?
text:
Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = fitted_m2, y = resid_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted rent", y = "Residual (actual − predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()

bptest(m2)

Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ___), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")

Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
This guided lab contains code blanks, so execution is off by default and the portfolio site can render it as a handout. After filling in the code, change eval: false to eval: true in this document’s YAML to run the chunks.
This is a Lab: it’s ungraded and done in class. You work in teams of 3–4.
Type the code. Don’t copy and paste it. Blanks look like ___. Fill them in, then run the chunk.
The first hour (Parts 1–5) is guided and builds your toolkit. The last part is the challenge: your team answers one policy question and defends one decision. At the end, the presenter from each team is chosen at random, so everyone needs to understand every step.

The question: Indego says it serves low-income Philadelphians. Which low-income tracts are farthest from a station, and how sure are we that they’re low-income?

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 0: Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)

# Your key lives in .Renviron. Never paste it here.
# tidycensus reads CENSUS_API_KEY automatically.
Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 1: The same pull as Week 3, plus one argument
text:
Part 1: The same pull as Week 3, plus one argument
This is the same get_acs() call you already know. The only new part is geometry = TRUE.

philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "___",
  variables = c(med_inc = "B19013_001",
                total_pop = "B01003_001"),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = ___
)

class(philly_tracts)
glimpse(philly_tracts)

Stop and look: What does class() show? Which column is new?
Now repeat the Week 3 steps. A data frame goes in, a data frame comes out. The geometry column comes along automatically.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    med_inc_se = med_incM / ___,
    med_inc_cv = (med_inc_se / med_incE) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      med_inc_cv < 12  ~ "High",
      med_inc_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Low"
    )
  )

# Did geometry survive? It should.
names(philly_tracts)

Your first map. It’s just ggplot with a new geom:

ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ___), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Median household income, Philadelphia tracts",
       fill = NULL)

Quick check: How many tracts have NA income even though they have people living in them? Write the code to count them.

philly_tracts %>%
  filter(is.na(___)) %>%
  nrow()

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 1b: Join by what
How much has income changed since 2015? Pull the older estimates. No geometry is needed, because this is just a table.

income_15 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(med_inc_15 = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2015,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = FALSE
) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_inc_15E, med_inc_15M)

nrow(income_15)
nrow(philly_tracts)

Stop and look: The row counts are different. Before you join, predict why.
Now join the 2015 table onto your tracts. The key is the column both tables share.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(income_15, by = "___")

nrow(philly_tracts)   # did the row count change?

The rule: after every join, count rows and count NAs.

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    no_2015_match = sum(is.na(___))
  )

Now look at which tracts failed to match:

# 2023 tracts with no 2015 partner
philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(is.na(med_inc_15E)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME) %>%
  head(10)

# 2015 tracts with no 2023 partner: anti_join keeps rows with NO match
income_15 %>%
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(philly_tracts), by = "GEOID") %>%
  head(10)

Discuss as a team: Did these places move? What changed between 2015 and 2023? Why can’t left_join() fix this? Keep your answer in mind; Part 3 comes back to it.






Note



Some NAs aren’t boundary changes. A tract can match but have NA income because the Census suppressed the estimate. How would you tell the two kinds of NA apart?

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 2: Bring in the stations
Indego publishes live station locations as GeoJSON. st_read() reads it directly from the URL.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE)

nrow(stations)
glimpse(stations)

Now check the CRS of both layers.

st_crs(philly_tracts)$epsg
st_crs(___)$epsg

Predict before you run: The two numbers are different. What will happen if you try to join them?

st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

That error is sf protecting you. Fix it by translating both layers into Pennsylvania South State Plane, EPSG 2272.






WarningLabel or translation?



st_set_crs() writes a label when the CRS is missing. st_transform() converts coordinates into a different CRS. Both layers here already have a CRS. Which function do you need?



philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>% ___(crs = 2272)
stations      <- stations %>% ___(crs = 2272)

st_crs(philly_tracts)$units   # what units are we in now?

Write down the units. Every number you type from now on is in these units.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 3: Join by where
In Part 1b, the join failed because it matched on a label (GEOID), and the label changed. st_join() matches on location instead: a row is matched to whatever it sits on top of. Stations don’t have a GEOID column, and they don’t need one.
Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

stations_with_tract <- st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(name, GEOID, med_incE, reliability) %>%
  head()

Now go the other way and count stations per tract. The first route is the Week 2 collapse pattern:

station_counts <- stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  ___(GEOID)

The second route counts directly:

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_intersects(., stations)))


Check your work

sum(philly_tracts$n_stations)
nrow(stations)

These probably don’t match. Discuss as a team: Why not? Find at least one station that explains the gap.
Hints: Look for stations where GEOID is NA in stations_with_tract. For double counts, look for stations that intersect more than one tract: which(lengths(st_intersects(stations, philly_tracts)) > 1).

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
text:
Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, ___)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = ___)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / ___
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = ___) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = ___)

nrow(outside_zone)

Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 6: The Challenge
You now have three different definitions of “has access”:

Distance: the tract centroid is within X miles of a station (dist_mi)
Touch: the tract touches the half-mile zone at all (st_filter)
Coverage: at least Y% of the tract’s area is inside the zone (pct_covered)


Your team’s task

Define “low-income.” For example, you could use the bottom quartile of tract median income, or a dollar threshold. Pick one and write it down.
Define “access.” Choose one of the three definitions above and set its threshold.
Answer the question. Which low-income tracts lack access? Produce:

The count of low-income tracts without access
A map showing them (a geom_sf() layer plus the stations)
The reliability breakdown: of those tracts, how many have High / Moderate / Low reliability income estimates?

Defend one decision in 2–3 sentences. Why this access definition and not another? How would your count change if you used a different one?
